notes: Delivery Logic levels. Map legend: docs/DELIVERY_RULES.md. min_pushes is proved by exhaustive BFS (tools/delivery_report.gd; re-checked by tests). 'design' is documentation only. 'mistake' is a push list from the start ([symbol, x, y, dir] = push the crate at x,y) that the report proves unsolvable. 'claims' are verified by constrained exhaustive search.

design.concept: Lesson: walking and pushing.
design.insight: A crate moves only away from the courier; to change its direction you walk round to another side.
design.mistake: Pushing the crate up against the top wall.
design.why: The top row has no coffee pad and a crate on a wall can never be pulled back off it (dead cell).

design.concept: Lesson: symbols. Each crate belongs on the pad with its own picture.
design.insight: The pad straight above each crate is the other crate's pad; the crates have to cross over.
design.mistake: Pushing each crate straight up onto the nearest pad.
design.why: A crate on the wrong pad does not count (the level stays unsolved); it can still be pushed off again, so this is a recoverable mistake, not a deadlock.

design.concept: Lesson: walls and corners trap crates; Undo is free.
design.insight: Route the crate down and along the open row; walls it does not need are dangerous.
design.mistake: Pushing the crate up onto the top wall (it starts right below it).
design.why: Proven dead cell: from the top row no push can ever bring the crate back down to the coffee pad. The game says so and offers Undo.

design.concept: Delivery order into a dead end, plus clearing the way.
design.insight: Both pads are in one dead-end shaft. The coffee pad is at the bottom, so coffee must go in first, and the croissant crate, which sits right above the shaft, has to step aside to let it pass.
design.mistake: Push the croissant (the closest crate) straight down the shaft onto its pad.
design.why: It is delivered, but the coffee crate can never get past it to the deeper pad. The position looks fine (nothing is stuck in a corner); only exhaustive search proves it unsolvable.
design.dependency: delivery order + temporary displacement (croissant moves aside first)

design.concept: Temporary displacement of an already-delivered crate.
design.insight: The croissant is home, but it stands where the coffee must come down. Push it away three cells (two leave you no room to get behind the coffee), deliver the coffee, then bring the croissant back.
design.mistake: Push the croissant one cell right and immediately drop the coffee into the gap.
design.why: The coffee now needs a push from the right, but that cell is the croissant's; and the croissant can only be pushed from where the coffee stands. Proven unsolvable.

design.concept: Do not seal a passage you will need: the closest delivery must wait.
design.insight: The croissant is one push from its pad, but its slot is the courier's way into the top room, and the top room is where you stand to push the coffee down onto its pad. Every solution moves the croissant away from its pad first (down, out of the slot) and brings it back at the end.
design.mistake: Deliver the croissant with the very first push.
design.why: The top room is sealed; the coffee can reach the cell above its pad but nobody can get above it to push it down. Proven unsolvable by search (no crate is visibly stuck).
design.dependency: preserving a route; temporary displacement; order

design.concept: Delivery order driven by access: the easiest delivery comes last.
design.insight: Coffee is one push from home, but its pad is the courier's only doorway to the top row, where it must stand to push the strawberry into the corner pad. Coffee goes last.
design.mistake: Push the coffee up onto its pad at once.
design.why: The top-right corner can no longer be reached from the left, so the strawberry can never be pushed right onto its pad. Proven by search.

design.concept: Order plus access: open the pocket before using it.
design.insight: The pads are stacked in the right-hand column, coffee at the bottom. To push coffee down onto it you must stand above it, reached only through the top-right pocket, which the croissant blocks. Move the croissant left first, deliver coffee, then bring the croissant round underneath.
design.mistake: Run the croissant right and down the column onto its pad.
design.why: Coffee can never reach the bottom pad behind it. Search proves it; nothing looks stuck.
design.dependency: delivery order; access side; temporary displacement

design.concept: Use an open route before it closes; displace a delivered crate far enough.
design.insight: The croissant needs a push from the top-left corner, but the coffee guards that corner. While the top row is open, walk round and push the coffee down two cells (one cell locks the route), deliver the croissant, then return the coffee and finish the strawberry.
design.mistake: Push the croissant up toward its pad first.
design.why: It closes the top row; the only way into the corner is now past the coffee, which can't be moved from below without jamming it into the corner. Proven by search.
design.dependency: preserving a route; temporary displacement; order

design.concept: A full delivery order through shared shafts.
design.insight: Coffee rides up the left shaft first (briefly crossing the croissant pad); the croissant then comes down the middle shaft and along the bottom row past the strawberry pad, so the strawberry, the closest crate, must be delivered last.
design.mistake: Deliver the strawberry first; it is only two pushes away.
design.why: With the strawberry home, the coffee crate next to it is pinned under the wall with nowhere to stand behind it: it can never move again (a provable freeze, reported at once).

design.concept: A tight three-way shuffle with a holding pocket.
design.insight: The middle row is the only highway and all three crates need it. Park the coffee in the pocket below, slide the strawberry past its own pad and back, and only lift the croissant once the highway is clear.
design.mistake: Push the croissant straight up toward its pad.
design.why: From the top row the croissant can only travel left, and it then walls the coffee's route. Proven by search.

design.concept: Compact challenge: a delivered crate at the crossroads.
design.insight: The croissant starts home, right at the bottom of the only shaft from the top room. Coffee goes up first; then the croissant steps up, down and away to the left so the strawberry can come down the shaft and through its pad, and finally returns.
design.mistake: Start the strawberry toward the shaft first.
design.why: It blocks the coffee's way up to its pad and then jams. Proven by search.
design.dependency: multi-step preparation; temporary displacement of a delivered crate; order

design.concept: Order in a single lane, and keeping a route open.
design.insight: In the top lane the croissant is in front, but its pad lies beyond the coffee pad: the croissant goes first and the coffee follows. Only then drop the strawberry down the gap; earlier, it cuts the lower lane, which is the only way round behind the coffee.
design.mistake: Step the croissant left, then drop the strawberry into the lower lane straight away.
design.why: The strawberry now blocks the lower lane, so the courier can never get behind the coffee again. Proven by search.

design.concept: A pad that is also a doorway (variation).
design.insight: The coffee's pad is the only way into the bottom-right corner, where you stand to push the strawberry left along the bottom row. Push the strawberry along first, then deliver the coffee, then sort out the croissant and the strawberry's last pushes.
design.mistake: Deliver the coffee straight down first.
design.why: The bottom-right corner is sealed, so the strawberry can only be pushed toward the right wall. Proven by search.

design.concept: Identical crates: choosing which crate goes to which pad.
design.insight: The coffee crate right next to the right-hand pad has to travel all the way to the left-hand pad; the other coffee crate then comes up and takes the near pad.
design.mistake: Push the nearest coffee crate onto the nearest pad.
design.why: The second coffee can then never be pushed along the top lane into the right corner: there is nowhere to stand behind it. Proven by search.
design.dependency: assignment of identical crates; temporary displacement

design.concept: Untangling a knot from the outside in.
design.insight: The croissant leaves first, down and round to its pad; that frees the coffee to step right and up onto its pad, and that frees the strawberry to drop onto its own.
design.mistake: Once the croissant has moved, slide the coffee left into the open gap.
design.why: The coffee is then stuck where it can never reach the coffee pad (an instant, provable dead cell).
design.dependency: delivery order (one of six crate orders works)

design.concept: Temporary displacement in a tight centre.
design.insight: The strawberry blocks the centre. It goes left and then up, away from its own pad, so the coffee can climb; then it comes back down past the coffee's column and the coffee steps up onto its pad.
design.mistake: Start by nudging the coffee left toward the centre.
design.why: The coffee now blocks the square the courier needs to move the strawberry out of the centre. Proven by search; nothing looks stuck.

design.concept: Displacing a delivered crate by exactly the right amount.
design.insight: To push the croissant down the left shaft you must stand on the coffee's pad. Slide the coffee two squares right (not three), bring the croissant round, send it down, slide the coffee back and finish.
design.mistake: Slide the coffee three squares right to make plenty of room.
design.why: From there it can't be brought back: the courier can no longer get to its right-hand side. Proven by search.
design.dependency: temporary displacement of a delivered crate

design.concept: The short way home blocks the stairs.
design.insight: The coffee is one push above its pad, but delivering it then walls the staircase the tea and croissant need. It takes the long way: right, down and back left, after the croissant and tea have used the stairs.
design.mistake: Push the coffee straight down onto its pad.
design.why: The staircase is cut, and the remaining crates can't all reach their pads. Proven by search.

design.concept: A one-way door: do the outside work first.
design.insight: The top coffee goes left to the top pad first. Pushing the inner coffee out of the little courtyard leaves the courier inside it, so that push comes after the outside work; then the croissant and the second coffee finish along the bottom row.
design.mistake: Push the inner coffee out of the courtyard first.
design.why: The courier ends up shut in the courtyard and can never reach the top coffee again. Proven by search.
design.dependency: delivery order; preserving a route (no single-crate order works)

design.concept: Clearing a shared road in the right order.
design.insight: The croissant clears the middle row first and parks below its pad; the coffee drops into the row and slides over above its pad; the strawberry drops out of the coffee's way; then all three finish.
design.mistake: Drop the coffee into the middle row first.
design.why: It jams against the croissant and the strawberry: all three are frozen and can never move again (an instant, provable freeze).

design.concept: Overshooting your own pad to clear a route.
design.insight: The tea must go down, along the middle row and up the left column. The coffee sits at the foot of that column, so it is pushed right, past its own pad, and only comes back once the tea has gone up.
design.mistake: Push the tea straight up into the top row toward its pad.
design.why: From the top row it could only be pushed left from the croissant's pad square, which the courier can't reach. Proven by search.

design.concept: Deep pad first, in an open room (variation).
design.insight: The coffee pad is in the corner below the croissant pad, so the coffee goes first: down and along the bottom-left row, briefly over the croissant pad, into the corner. The croissant must keep out of the left column until then.
design.mistake: Push the croissant into the left column on the way to its pad.
design.why: Once the croissant is in the column it can only go down onto its pad, which seals the coffee's corner. Proven by search.

design.concept: Identical crates with crossing routes.
design.insight: The right-hand coffee climbs the right column to the top pad; the croissant goes round by the left column; only then does the left-hand coffee cross the middle row to the bottom pad.
design.mistake: Start by pushing the left-hand coffee toward the right.
design.why: It jams against the other coffee: both are frozen and neither can move again (an instant, provable freeze).

design.concept: Displacement with a timed return.
design.insight: The croissant steps down out of the lane; the top coffee goes left through the croissant's pad into the far corner; the croissant then starts back up BEFORE the bottom coffee is delivered, because its return needs the square that coffee will fill.
design.mistake: As soon as the croissant is out of the way, deliver the bottom coffee.
design.why: The croissant can never come back up: the courier can no longer stand below it. Proven by search.

design.concept: A shuttle crate: past its pad, away, and back.
design.insight: The croissant goes past its pad so the tea can be pushed up from below, then all the way back left so the courier can get round; in the shortest solution it is delivered last, after the strawberry has passed along the middle row.
design.mistake: Push the strawberry along the middle row toward its corner first.
design.why: The courier can no longer get below the tea to push it up. Proven by search.

design.concept: A delivered crate as a gate you open and close.
design.insight: Open the gate: once the croissant is in the middle row, push the coffee up two squares, use the bottom row to get under the croissant and lift it into the right column, then close the gate again before the strawberry comes through.
design.mistake: Lift the coffee up one square at the start.
design.why: It now stands on the strawberry's pad and the croissant can't get past. Proven by search.
design.dependency: temporary displacement; order; preserving a route

design.concept: Two crates swapping sides through a single crossroads.
design.insight: The croissant steps left so the coffee can come up and right; the croissant then ducks into the alcove's mouth to let the coffee pass back left; in the shortest solution the coffee goes down the left column to its pad first, and the croissant climbs to the top row and finishes.
design.mistake: Run the croissant all the way left into the left column.
design.why: It would be delivered by going up, but it blocks the coffee's only way down the left column. Proven by search.

design.concept: A long multi-step preparation through one door.
design.insight: The strawberry steps off its pad and out of the way; the tea comes through the door and round to its corner; the coffee follows through the door to its pad; the strawberry goes the long way round the right room and back home last.
design.mistake: Push the strawberry right, toward the door.
design.why: It jams against the coffee and the tea beside the door: all three are frozen and can never move again (an instant, provable freeze).

design.concept: Final challenge: interlocking routes.
design.insight: The strawberry shuffles out of the bottom row, the coffee steps up and back down to let the croissant into the middle column, the croissant climbs to the top row and is delivered along it, and the coffee drops onto its pad last.
design.mistake: Push the croissant right onto the coffee pad, toward the middle.
design.why: It jams the bottom row that the other two crates need. Proven by search.
